title: Opinion of the European Central Bank of 16 April 2026 on the obligation to accept cash payments and the obligation of credit institutions to provide cash services (CON/2026/14)
text:
EN
ECB-PUBLIC
OPINION OF THE EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK
of 16 April 2026
on the obligation to accept cash payments and the obligation of credit institutions to provide cash
services
(CON/2026/14)
Introduction and legal basis
On 12 March 2026, the Swedish Government submitted a legislative proposal (hereinafter the ‘legislative
proposal’) to the Swedish Parliament on measures to strengthen the functioning of cash, containing a draft
law on an obligation for retail grocery stores and pharmacies to accept cash payments (hereinafter the ‘draft
law’) and draft amendments to the Law on payment services1 (hereinafter the ‘draft amendments’, and
together with the draft law, the ‘draft legislative provisions’).
The European Central Bank (ECB) has decided to deliver an own initiative opinion on the draft legislative
provisions. The ECB’s competence to deliver an opinion is based on Articles 127(4) and 282(5) of the
Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Article 2(1), second indent, of Council Decision
98/415/EC2, as the draft legislative provisions relate to means of payment. In accordance with Article 17.5,
first sentence, of the Rules of Procedure of the European Central Bank, the Governing Council has adopted
this opinion.
1.
Purpose of the draft legislative provisions
1.1
The overarching purpose of the draft legislative provisions is to safeguard the functionality of cash
as a means of payment. As noted in the legislative proposal, in order for cash to be a functioning
means of payment, it must be possible to pay with cash, especially for goods and services that are
of the most basic nature3.
1.2
Role of cash in Swedish society
1.2.1 According to the legislative proposal, the use of cash in Sweden is declining rapidly in society as a
result of, among other things, new, simpler and cheaper card payment services and a sharp increase
in instant payments, not least in the form of the Swish service. In June 2023, cash accounted for just
under 0.9 % of the money circulating in the economy as a share of gross domestic product (GDP),
compared with 1.16 % in 2020 and 2.74 % in 2010. As for Swedish people’s payment habits, in 2023
the vast majority of payments in Sweden, measured by number of transactions, were made by card,
followed by Swish. Cash payments between private individuals have largely been replaced by Swish.
1
Lagen (2010:751) om betaltjänster.
2
Council Decision 98/415/EC of 29 June 1998 on the consultation of the European Central Bank by national authorities
regarding draft legislative provisions (OJ L 189, 3.7.1998, p. 42, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dec/1998/415/oj).
3
See page 1 of the legislative proposal.
2
ECB-PUBLIC
Today, approximately one in ten purchases in shops is made with cash, compared with one in four
purchases in 20104.
1.2.2 Despite the decline in cash usage, the legislative proposal notes that several surveys show that the
majority of the Swedish population wants to keep cash. In Bankomat AB's survey on the general
public's attitude to cash, conducted in spring 2024, 83 % responded that they want to keep cash as
a possible means of payment in the future, while 11 % wanted to see a completely cashless society.
There were no major differences between men and women's attitudes, but older people were keener
to keep cash, while younger people were more positive about a cashless society, although a majority
in all age groups wanted to keep cash. According to Sveriges Riksbank’s survey of Swedish people's
payment habits from 2023, 44 % are negative or very negative about the increasing decline in the
use of cash in Sweden. When asked whether they could manage without cash in society as it is
today, 31 % said they could not manage without cash5.
1.2.3 According to the legislative proposal, the possibility of paying with cash varies between different
businesses and different parts of the country. According to Sveriges Riksbank’s Payments Report
20256, 71 % of companies in the retail sector, as well as restaurants and hairdressers, accept cash.
Significantly more companies that sell everyday goods accept cash than those that sell infrequently
purchased goods. According to a 2024 survey by Svensk Handel (the Swedish Trade Federation),
91 % of retailers accept cash payments, which is 20 percentage points higher than shown in Sveriges
Riksbank's survey7. The survey also shows that 97 % of grocery stores accept cash payments. The
most important factor behind whether companies accept cash is whether customers demand it,
according to Sveriges Riksbank’s Payments Report 2025. Additional reasons that many companies
consider important are that they want to include certain customers and be prepared for crises and
war. Of the companies that do not accept cash, just over 40 % have stopped accepting cash in the
last five years, while 40 % say they have never accepted cash. The main reason to stop accepting
cash is the security risk, followed by the time it takes to handle cash and, finally, difficulties in
depositing daily takings8.
1.2.4 According to the legislative proposal, the special status of cash derives not only from the fact that it
is legal tender provided by the State, whose value is ultimately guaranteed by the State, but also
from the fact that cash, in its physical form, has certain characteristics that few other means of
payment have. Cash is a more accessible means of payment for people who, for various reasons,
cannot use digital means of payment. Cash can also be a useful means of payment in situations
where individuals need assistance to make purchases and do not handle the payment themselves.
Cash also has a function in terms of preparedness as one of several means of payment. In order to
guarantee the functioning of cash in the event of disruptions, it is essential that structures are in place
4
See Section 4.2 of the legislative proposal.
5
See Section 4.2.1 of the legislative proposal.
6
Available on Sveriges Riksbank’s website at www.riksbank.se.
7
See Section 1.3 of Sveriges Riksbank’s Payments Report 2025, available on Sveriges Riksbank’s website at
www.riksbank.se.

See Section 4.2.2 of the legislative proposal.
3
ECB-PUBLIC
that can be maintained under normal conditions, so that cash can be one of several means of
payment available during heightened preparedness or peacetime crisis situations9.
1.2.5 Despite the obligation for credit institutions to provide cash services, which entered into force on 1
January 2021, cash usage has continued to decline. If access to cash continues to decline, cash
may eventually risk losing its real significance as a means of payment. There is therefore a risk that
it will not be possible to ensure in the future the objective set by the Parliament and the Government
that everyone in society should have access to basic payment services at reasonable prices. Such
a development would pose serious problems for society, not only in terms of exclusion and lack of
integrity for parts of the population, but also in terms of security, preparedness and efficiency in the
payment market. Against this background, the Government considers it important to safeguard the
functionality of cash as a means of payment10.
1.3
Obligation of retail grocery stores and pharmacies to accept cash payments
1.3.1 The draft law obliges retail grocery stores and pharmacies to accept cash as payment for the sale of
goods and services at physical points of sale with staffed cash registers. Further, banknotes and
coins are considered as cash, and the obligation applies to payments of up to 0.1 of the ‘price base
amount’11, which in 2026 is equal to kronor (SEK) 5 920 (approximately EUR 53812), and not more
than 25 coins13. As noted in the legislative proposal, the draft law is self-regulatory in nature as there
is no supervisory authority, and the operators covered by the obligation to accept cash payments
decide how to comply with it. The draft law does not apply to the legal relationship between the
operator covered by the obligation and the operator's customers, i.e. the draft law is not a civil law
regulation that gives an individual customer the right to pay with cash, but rather an obligation for the
operator, with certain limitations and exceptions, to accept cash payments from its customers14.
Further, at points of sale where the obligation applies, cash must be accepted for the purchase of all
goods or services sold in pharmacies or retail grocery stores, i.e. not only food and medicines
respectively15. Some consultation bodies have raised questions about the risk of money laundering.
However, the Government notes that the purpose of an obligation to accept cash payments is to
ensure that the most basic goods and services can be paid for in cash. There is therefore no need
to make larger cash payments. The Government therefore considers that an amount limit should be
introduced to reduce the risk that the obligation will lead to a significant increase in daily cash
balances in relation to current levels that could present an attractive target for criminal actors and
entail significant cost increases in respect of cash handling. The limit therefore reduces the risk of
money laundering. Grocery stores within retail and pharmacies will therefore continue to have the
option, but not the obligation, to accept larger cash payments16.
9
See Section 5 of the legislative proposal.
10
See Section 5 of the legislative proposal.
11
The price base amount is an amount set annually by Statistics Sweden reflecting price trends (inflation) in society and
is used to calculate various taxes, subsidies and fees. Statistics Sweden’s website at www.scb.se.
12
Based on the euro reference rate for the krona on 7 April 2026, SEK 5 920 is equivalent to EUR 538,67. The euro
reference rate for the krona published by the ECB is available on the ECB’s website at www.ecb.europa.eu.
13
See Section 1 of the draft law and Section 2.1 of the legislative proposal.
14
See Section 11.1 of the legislative proposal.
15
See Section 11.1 of the legislative proposal.

See Section 5 of the legislative proposal.
4
ECB-PUBLIC
1.3.2 Furthermore, the obligation to accept cash payments does not apply if it leads to an inability to (a)
maintain security at the point of sale, or (b) continue the operation of the point of sale due to the
costs of cash handling17. The limitation set out in (a) means that the obligation only applies to grocery
stores within retail and pharmacies where the safety of staff can be maintained by reasonable means.
As noted in the legislative proposal, a store or pharmacy is therefore not required to accept cash
payments in the evening or at night if the store or pharmacy has such opening hours and it is not
possible to maintain staff safety during these opening hours. In places where the risk of the shop or
pharmacy being exposed to robbery or other crime is high even during the day, the obligation does
not apply at any time of the day18. The limitation set out in (b) means that the obligation does not
apply if the cost of cash handling is so high that there is a risk that retail grocery stores and
pharmacies will have to close, thereby leading to a deterioration in service19.
1.3.3 Moreover, retail grocery stores and pharmacies may refuse to accept cash payments in respect of
individual sales if there is an acceptable reason to do so20. As noted in the legislative proposal, this
may arise if, for example, temporary circumstances make it impossible to accept cash payments for
individual sales. This may be the case, for example, if the cash register is full and the point of sale
cannot accept any more banknotes or coins, or if a customer makes repeated purchases within a
limited period in a way that is incompatible with the purpose of the obligation. Retail grocery stores
and pharmacies may not, however, refuse to accept cash payments arbitrarily21.
1.4
Obligation of credit institutions to provide cash services
1.4.1 The draft amendments provide that credit institutions and branches of foreign credit institutions that
provide payment accounts with basic functionalities to consumers and services that enable cash to
be withdrawn from these accounts (cash withdrawal points) to an adequate extent throughout the
country must also provide services that enable cash to be deposited in these accounts (cash deposit
points)22. As noted in the legislative proposal, credit institutions are currently required to provide
facilities for depositing cash to businesses, but not to consumers. The services for businesses are
also available to consumers to a certain extent, and deposit machines, for example, are widely used
by consumers. As fewer bank branches handle cash, deposit machines have become more important
in allowing consumers to deposit cash. Since the obligation to provide cash services was introduced
in 2021, the proportion of the population that lives more than 25 kilometres from the nearest location
for both withdrawals and deposits has decreased, but, at the same time, so has the number of
locations. Against this background, the Government considers that credit institutions should also be
required to provide locations for cash deposits for consumers. The purpose of this would be to ensure
a minimum level of consumer access to cash services throughout the country, regardless of demand.
This is also in line with the Union’s objective that all consumers in a Member State should have
access to such services without having to travel far from their homes to reach them. The same
geographical distribution that applies to the provision of locations for daily cash deposits for
17
See Section 2 of the draft law.
18
See Section 11.1 of the legislative proposal.
19
See Section 5 of the legislative proposal.
20
See Section 3 of the draft law and Section 2.1 of the legislative proposal.
21
See Section 5 and Section 11.1 of the legislative proposal.
22
See Chapter 9, Section 1, of the draft amendments and Section 2.2 of the legislative proposal.

ECB-PUBLIC
businesses should apply to locations for cash deposits for consumers, i.e. no more than 1.22 % of
the population should have to travel more than 25 kilometres to the nearest location for cash
deposits23. In practice, cash deposit locations will coincide with locations for daily cash deposits for
businesses. The functional meaning of this obligation is therefore – as for locations for daily cash
deposits – that locations for cash deposits for consumers must be accessible, i.e. have reasonable
opening hours and fees and be user-friendly, for example for to take account of people’s functional
diversity. This does not mean that credit institutions and branches must provide cash deposit facilities
for consumers on their own premises, as the obligation may instead be fulfilled through other
companies that provide cash service facilities. This means that a location for cash services that is
accessible to the customers of several credit institutions and branches may fulfil the obligation to
provide cash services for a specific geographical area for all of these credit institutions and
branches24.
1.4.2 The draft amendments provide that credit institutions and branches of foreign credit institutions that
had retail deposits amounting to over SEK 70 billion (equal to approximately EUR 6,4 billion25) on
1 July of the preceding year and that provide payment accounts to companies must provide services
that enable cash to be deposited in these accounts (daily deposit taking points) to an adequate extent
throughout the country and must also provide companies with adequate and appropriate services for
handling change and daily deposit takings26. As noted in the legislative proposal, safeguarding the
functionality of cash as a means of payment requires access to services that enable the taking of
daily deposits. When a central part of the infrastructure is provided solely by an operator that, under
current regulations, has no obligation to provide these services, the cash chain becomes vulnerable.
If Loomis Sverige AB, which is essentially the only current operator, were to cease its operations in
this area, there would be a risk that daily cash deposits would only be available via daily cash deposit
locations (deposit machines) that have limits on the amount that can be deposited. The Government
considers that credit institutions should take greater responsibility for offering the daily cash deposit
services required to maintain a functioning cash infrastructure. The Government also considers it
important that the cash chain should be maintained. Credit institutions should therefore provide
appropriate and needs-based services for daily cash deposits. However, the Government also
considers that the obligation to provide locations for daily cash deposits should remain in order to
continue to ensure that services are spread throughout the country. The proposed arrangement thus
supplements the existing obligation, clarifying that credit institutions should, to a greater extent than
today, provide the services for daily cash deposits that companies receiving cash payments need in
order to reduce the vulnerability of the infrastructure and enable continued cash acceptance. It is
also important that credit institutions support the circulation of cash in society, as this helps to
maintain confidence in credit institutions and the monetary system. The Government further
considers that access to cash handling services is a prerequisite for businesses to be able to handle
cash payments. The Government also considers it important to safeguard the functionality of cash

See Section 6.1 of the legislative proposal.
24
See Section 11.2 of the legislative proposal.
25
Based on the euro reference rate for the krona on 7 April 2026, SEK 70 billion is equivalent to EUR 6,369 billion. The
euro reference rate for the krona published by the ECB is available on the ECB’s website at www.ecb.europa.eu.
26
See Chapter 9, Section 1a, of the draft amendments and Section 2.2 of the legislative proposal.
6
ECB-PUBLIC
as a means of payment and this requires access to services that enable businesses to accept cash
payments, such as access to appropriate and needs-based cash handling services. The Government
therefore considers that credit institutions should provide appropriate and needs-based cash
handling services. The draft amendments should be self-regulatory in nature, which means that it is
up to the individual credit institution to decide how to fulfil it. Several consultation bodies point out
that the draft amendments increase the risk of money laundering and robbery. However, in the
Government's view, the draft amendments are designed in such a way that they give credit
institutions scope to take these risks into account when fulfilling the obligations in question27.
1.4.3 Pursuant to the draft amendments, the possibility of the Government or the authority appointed by
the Government to adopt provisions for the purpose of the application of the provisions described in
paragraphs 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 must, in addition to including the maximum number of individuals who
may have a certain maximum road distance in kilometres between their registered address and the
nearest cash withdrawal point, also include cash deposit points and daily deposit taking points.
1.4.4 Currently, the Law on payment services provides that if a credit institution or a branch of foreign
credit institution does not fulfil its obligations as described in paragraphs 1.4.1 and 1.4.2, the Post-
och telestyrelsen (Swedish Post and Telecom Authority), which supervises credit institutions and
branches of foreign credit institutions in respect of the abovementioned obligations, must transfer the
matter to Finansinspektionen (SFSA, Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority). The SFSA may then
require the credit institution to take corrective action within a certain time, and if the credit institution
does not comply with the relevant requirement within such time, the SFSA may decide that the credit
institution must pay an administrative fee. Pursuant to the draft amendments these powers will now
also apply in respect of the obligations to accept cash deposits and to provide adequate and
appropriate services for handling change and daily deposit takings28.
1.5
Entry into force
It is proposed that the draft legislative provisions will enter into force on 1 July 202629.
2.
Role and importance of cash payments in society
2.1
The ECB strongly welcomes the basic objective of the draft legislative provisions to safeguard the
functionality of cash as a means of payment in Sweden. The ECB understands that electronic
payment instruments continue increasingly to be used as a method of payment in Sweden, while the
use of cash continues to decline. Although electronic payment instruments are increasingly used for
retail payments in a number of Member States, cash continues to play an important role in society
and is still widely used throughout the entire population. As the ECB has noted previously, cash is
secure, widely accepted, fast and facilitates control over the payer’s spending. Moreover, it is
currently the only payment instrument that allows citizens to settle a transaction instantly and directly
27
See Section 6.2 of the legislative proposal.
28
See Chapter 9, Sections 2, 4 and 5, of the Law on payment services.
29
See Section 2.1 and 2.2 of the legislative proposal.
7
ECB-PUBLIC
between two parties in central bank money, while ensuring privacy30. Cash payments facilitate the
inclusion of the entire population in the economy by allowing it to settle any kind of financial
transaction in this way, thus ensuring freedom of choice as to the method of payment for all citizens31.
2.2
The ECB agrees that the ability to pay in cash remains particularly important for those who, for
various legitimate reasons, prefer to use physical money for payments rather than other payment
instruments, or do not have access to the banking system and electronic means of payment. These
groups include not only elderly people but also people with disabilities, immigrants, socially
vulnerable people, minors and others with limited or no access to digital payment services32.
Furthermore, cash may play an important role in the event of a disturbance in the payment system33
and it is robust against cybercrime34 and power outages as it guarantees person-to-person payment
transactions in such situations. Cash also has an important function as a store of value. The
availability and accessibility of cash and its fallback function in case of disruptions to electronic
payment systems contribute to trust in the financial system, which is important for the smooth
functioning of monetary policy35.
3.
Obligation of credit institutions to provide cash services
3.1
The ECB has previously welcomed the introduction of the requirement applying to certain Swedish
credit institutions, as well as certain Swedish branches of foreign credit institutions, to provide cash
services to consumers and firms, for the purpose of facilitating the continued use of cash in Sweden
by ensuring an adequate level of access to cash services throughout Sweden36. While the official
currency in Sweden is the krona, not the euro, the ECB considers it important that all Member States,
including non-euro area Member States, take appropriate measures to ensure that credit institutions
and branches operating within their territories provide adequate access to cash services, in order to

facilitate the continued use of cash37. Sufficient and effective access to cash is necessary to preserve
the effectiveness of the legal tender status of cash. If citizens do not have easy access to cash, they
will not be able to use it as a means of payment and store of value38. Against this backdrop, the ECB
welcomes the draft amendments, which expand the obligation of credit institutions to provide cash
services.
3.2
The ECB notes that that an adequate level of access to cash services should guarantee reasonable
and proportionate cash service networks to avoid that citizens have problems accessing their money
in cash39. In addition, the ECB wishes to note that a minimum level of over-the counter, in-person
cash withdrawal services at branches may be needed at credit institutions, especially for those
groups in society that do not have access to electronic means of payment. Such over-the-counter,
in-person cash withdrawal services would also enable access to cash in situations where automated
teller machine networks are temporarily unavailable. Moreover, customers should have sufficient and
effective access to cash deposit services at credit institutions, both at bank counters and cash deposit
machines, for banknotes and coins. This would support the acceptance of cash by payees (e.g.
merchants and public sector entities) by ensuring that they can conveniently convert cash into
commercial bank money and manage their liquidity efficiently, for instance to pay their suppliers and
employees40.
3.3
The ECB welcomes the administrative fees that may be imposed by the SFSA on credit institutions
under the draft amendments, which should facilitate the enforcement of their obligations under the
draft amendments41.
4.
Obligation to accept cash payments
4.1
Status of krona banknotes and coins as legal tender
In Sweden, krona cash and emergency money are legal tender42, meaning that everyone is obliged
to accept banknotes and coins as payment. However, as noted in the explanatory memorandum to
the Law on Sveriges Riksbank, this obligation may be waived by agreement in civil law relationships
or certain public law relationships of a civil law nature. Exceptions to this obligation may also be
made in legislation43.
4.2
Status of euro banknotes and coins as legal tender
4.2.1 Although Member States with a derogation, including Sweden, do not yet participate in the third stage
of economic and monetary union, they have a legal duty to adapt the statutes of their national central

ECB-PUBLIC
banks (NCBs) to ensure compatibility with the Treaty44 and the Statute of the European System of
Central Banks and of the European Central Bank (hereinafter the ‘Statute of the ESCB’). Any
legislative reform in any such Member State should aim to gradually achieve consistency with ESCB
standards45. Furthermore, although Union law only regulates the legal tender status of euro
banknotes and coins, the Union framework applicable to the legal tender status of euro banknotes
and coins will become directly applicable in Sweden if and when the euro is introduced in Sweden.
Against this institutional backdrop, the ECB has prepared an assessment of the draft law’s provisions
compared with relevant practices in the euro area, in particular as concerns the legal tender status
of euro banknotes.
4.2.2 The ECB has the exclusive right to authorise the issue of euro banknotes within the Union, and the
euro banknotes issued by the ECB and the NCBs of the euro area are the only banknotes with legal
tender status within the euro area46. The legal tender status of euro coins is provided for in secondary
Union law47.
4.2.3 The concept of ‘legal tender’ as a means of payment denominated in a currency unit has been
considered by the Court of Justice of the European Union. In particular, the Court of Justice clarified
that the concept of ‘legal tender’ signifies that this specific means of payment cannot generally be
refused in settlement of a debt, denominated in the same currency unit at its full-face value, with the
effect of discharging the debt. In clarifying the concept of ‘legal tender’ under Union law, the Court of
Justice took into consideration Commission Recommendation 2010/191/EU48, which provides useful
guidance for the interpretation of the relevant provisions of Union law. Point 1 of Recommendation
2010/191 states that, where a payment obligation exists, the legal tender of euro banknotes and
coins should imply: (a) mandatory acceptance of those banknotes and coins; (b) their acceptance at
full face value; and (c) their power to discharge from payment obligations. According to the Court of
Justice, this shows that the concept of ‘legal tender’ encompasses, inter alia, an obligation in principle
to accept banknotes and coins denominated in euro for payment purposes49.
4.2.4 However, the Court of Justice further clarified that the status of legal tender calls only for acceptance
in principle of banknotes and coins denominated in euro as a means of payment, not for absolute
acceptance. The Union’s exclusive competence in matters of monetary policy is without prejudice to
the competence of the Member States whose currency is the euro to regulate the procedures for
settling pecuniary obligations, provided, in particular, that the legislation does not affect the principle
that, as a general rule, it must be possible to discharge a payment obligation in cash. Thus, that
exclusive competence does not prevent a Member State from adopting a measure falling within one
of the Member State’s competences. For instance, a Member State may, based on its competence

to organise its public administration, oblige the public administration to accept cash payments from
citizens. Neither does it prevent a Member State, in the exercise of its own powers, from introducing,
on legitimate public interest grounds, a derogation from that obligation for statutorily imposed
payments, subject to compliance with certain conditions. In particular, the obligation to accept euro
banknotes and coins may, in principle, be restricted by the Member States for reasons of public
interest and subject to the principle of proportionality. This means that any such restrictions must be
proportionate to the public interest objective pursued. When limiting the possibility, recognised by
Union law, of generally discharging a payment obligation in banknotes and coins denominated in
euro, Member States must ensure that all measures comply with the principle of proportionality,
which requires in particular that they are appropriate for achieving the legitimate objectives pursued
by the legislation at issue and do not go beyond what is necessary in order to achieve those
objectives50.
4.2.5 The Court of Justice has established that restrictions of the legal tender status of euro banknotes in
particular require that the legislation (a) does not have the object or effect of establishing legal rules
governing the status of legal tender of euro banknotes; (b) does not lead, in law or in fact, to abolition
of those banknotes, in particular by calling into question the possibility, as a general rule, of
discharging a payment obligation in cash; (c) has been adopted for reasons of public interest; (d)
only entails a limitation on cash payments that is appropriate for attaining the public interest objective
pursued; and (e) only entails a limitation on cash payments that does not go beyond what is
necessary in order to achieve the public interest objective51.
4.2.6 Regarding the proportionality of a restriction of the legal tender status of euro banknotes, the Court
requires not only that the measure is appropriate for attaining the public interest objective pursued,
but also that it must not go beyond what is necessary in order to achieve that objective. The ECB
has undertaken additional reflection in its opinions with respect to whether limitations may be
considered proportionate52. In particular, the ECB has noted that the broader and more general a
limitation is, the stricter the interpretation of the proportionality requirement should be. When
considering whether a limitation is proportionate, the adverse impact of the limitation in question and
whether alternative measures capable of fulfilling the relevant objective with a less adverse impact
should always be considered53.
4.2.7 The Court of Justice has clarified that the concept of ‘legal tender’ is a concept of Union law that
must be given an autonomous and uniform interpretation throughout the Union54. It has also
established that Article 133 of the Treaty empowers the Union legislature alone to specify the legal
rules governing the status of legal tender accorded to banknotes and coins denominated in euro,
insofar as that is necessary for the use of the euro as the single currency. Furthermore, the Union

legislature’s exclusive competence precludes any competence on the part of the Member States in

banknotes and coins56 (hereinafter the ‘proposed regulation on the legal tender of euro cash’), which

The explanatory memorandum accompanying the proposed regulation on the legal tender of euro
cash states that discussions within the Euro Legal Tender Expert Group (ELTEG) confirmed the
existence of legal uncertainty regarding the legal tender of euro cash and differing application of its
principles in the euro area57. These differences would justify establishing rules on the legal tender of
euro cash in a regulation adopted under Article 133 of the Treaty.
4.3
Specific observations regarding the draft law’s provisions on the obligation to accept cash payments
4.3.1 The ECB understands that the obligation to accept cash payments refers to payments executed in
the legal tender of Sweden. It must be considered whether the obligation to accept cash in the draft
law, if and when the euro is introduced as Sweden’s legal tender, would establish legal rules
governing the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins, which is an area of exclusive
competence of the Union under Article 133 of the Treaty, or whether it is a measure taken in the
exercise of the competence of the Member States.
4.3.2 The draft law’s obligation to accept cash is limited to business-to-consumer transactions. It does not
extend to cases in which the debtor of the pecuniary debt is not a consumer (e.g. business-to-
business transactions) or in which both the creditor and the debtor are consumers (i.e. consumer-to-
consumer transactions). The ECB therefore understands that the obligation to accept cash set out in
the draft law is intended as a national measure that regulates the procedures for settling pecuniary
obligations in the exercise of national powers, particularly in the field of consumer protection. The
draft law would not seem to establish legal rules governing the status of legal tender of euro
banknotes and coins, which would become relevant if and when the euro is introduced as Sweden’s
legal tender.
4.3.3 As regards the limitation on the obligation to accept cash payments in the event of the inability to
maintain security at the point of sale (see paragraph 1.3.2), the ECB notes the absence of clear,
objective and narrowly defined criteria to determine when such a security risk may be held to arise.
There is accordingly a risk of inconsistent application or overly broad interpretations that may restrict
the acceptance of cash payments, especially given the absence of a public enforcement mechanism
under the draft law. This lack of precision may create legal uncertainty, undermining the predictability
and uniformity of the legal framework governing cash acceptance58.

4.3.4 In relation to the fact that the limitation on the obligation to accept cash payments due to the inability
to maintain security at the point of sale (see paragraph 1.3.2) may be applied during evening or
nighttime hours, the ECB notes that retail grocery stores and pharmacies are essential services that
often serve individuals who rely on the ability to pay in cash. A number of social groups, such as shift
workers, tourists, individuals without access to electronic payment methods, or those who prefer to
use cash for budgeting purposes or for any other legitimate reason, may prefer using cash to pay for
necessary goods also during these hours.
4.3.5 As regards the limitation on the obligation to accept cash payments in respect of individual sales if
there is an acceptable reason to do so (see paragraph 1.3.3), the ECB notes – similarly to the
limitation related to the inability to maintain security at the point of sale – that both the existence of
the limitation itself and the absence of clear, objective and narrowly defined criteria related to its
application may create a risk of inconsistent application or overly broad interpretations that may
restrict the acceptance of cash payments, especially given the absence of a public enforcement
mechanism under the draft law59.
4.3.6 The legislative proposal states that the draft law is self-regulatory in nature as there is no supervisory
authority, and it is the operators covered by the obligation to accept cash payments who decide how
to comply with it (see paragraph 1.3.1). It is therefore doubtful whether the draft law effectively
achieves the objective of safeguarding the functionality of cash as a means of payment. In this
context, the ECB notes that a lack of public supervision over the application of the limitations provided
for in the draft law could undermine cash acceptance60.
